chapters.name: Hadean
chapters.lede: Earth assembles out of the debris around a young Sun, is hit by a planet, and cools just enough to hold an ocean.
story: The Earth grows by collision. Rock and metal left over from the Sun’s formation clump into ever larger bodies until, within about 100 million years, one of them is our planet. The energy of all that infalling matter has nowhere to go, so the surface is molten: a magma ocean hundreds of kilometres deep, under a thick atmosphere of steam and carbon dioxide, lit by a Sun about 30% fainter than today’s.

Then something the size of Mars hits. The impact strips away a huge volume of Earth’s mantle, re-melts what is left, and the debris settles into orbit and coalesces into the Moon — which at first hangs perhaps fifteen times closer than it does now, raising enormous tides and pulling the young Earth’s day down to a few hours.

Cooling is faster than the name "Hadean" suggests. Zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, some of them 4.4 billion years old, formed in granite-like melts in the presence of liquid water. Within roughly 150 million years of the Moon-forming impact there is already an ocean, a crust, and a chemistry set running on a global scale.
chapters.world: No continents in any modern sense — only scraps of proto-crust floating on a mantle far hotter than today’s, repeatedly resurfaced by impacts and eruptions.

events.title: The Solar System begins
events.text: The oldest solids in meteorites — calcium-aluminium inclusions — condense. This date is the zero point for the age of everything else.

events.title: The Moon-forming impact
events.text: A Mars-sized body, usually called Theia, strikes the proto-Earth. The Moon forms from the debris within a century or so, and Earth’s spin axis and day length are set.

events.title: Liquid water
events.text: The Jack Hills zircons record granitic melts and water-rock interaction — the oldest direct evidence that Earth had an ocean and something like a crust.

events.title: Possible earliest life
events.text: Graphite grains in Jack Hills zircons, and later carbon in Greenland rocks, carry the light carbon signature that life leaves behind. The evidence is contested but persistent.

chapters.name: Archean
chapters.lede: For a billion and a half years the planet is inhabited, warm, and almost completely airless in the sense that matters to us: no oxygen.
story: By 3.5 billion years ago life is unmistakable. Stromatolites — layered mounds built by mats of microbes trapping sediment — appear in Western Australia and South Africa, and their descendants still grow in Shark Bay today. The metabolisms of the time run on hydrogen, iron, sulphur and methane. Photosynthesis exists but does not yet split water.

The atmosphere is nitrogen and carbon dioxide with a great deal of methane and no free oxygen. The Sun is still 20–25% dimmer than today, yet there is no global glaciation for most of this eon — the "faint young Sun paradox", resolved by a much stronger greenhouse.

Continents are being made. Small cratons — the ancient cores of every modern continent, from the Pilbara to the Kaapvaal to the Superior — weld together out of volcanic arcs and greenstone belts. Some time in this eon, cyanobacteria invent oxygenic photosynthesis, and the oxygen they release is soaked up by dissolved iron, which settles out as the banded iron formations that supply most of the world’s iron ore.
chapters.world: Dozens of small, hot cratons in a global ocean. Plate tectonics is starting up, but the crust is thinner and the mantle hotter, so the style is not quite the modern one.

events.title: The oldest rock
events.text: The Acasta Gneiss in northwest Canada — the oldest intact piece of continental crust yet dated, and the marker that now defines the base of the Archean.

events.title: Isua
events.text: Banded iron and pillow lavas in Greenland record deep water, and carbon isotopes there are widely read as biological.

events.title: Stromatolites
events.text: The Dresser Formation of the Pilbara preserves microbial mounds, and with them the oldest broadly accepted fossils.

events.title: Oxygenic photosynthesis
events.text: Cyanobacteria begin splitting water for hydrogen and dumping oxygen as waste. It will take the better part of a billion years for that waste to accumulate.

events.title: Cratons stabilise
events.text: A pulse of continental growth builds the cores of most modern continents.

featured.name: Cyanobacteria
featured.note: The organism that changed the atmosphere: the first to split water for hydrogen and release oxygen as waste.

featured.name: Stromatolite
featured.note: Not a species but a structure — layered rock built up by microbial mats, and the dominant fossil of the Precambrian.

featured.name: Archaea
featured.note: A whole domain of life adapted to heat, salt and sulphur, and the lineage our own cells’ ancestor came from.

chapters.name: Paleoproterozoic
chapters.lede: Oxygen floods the air, nearly everything alive is poisoned, the planet freezes — and the complex cell is invented.
story: Around 2.4 billion years ago, free oxygen finally overwhelms the chemical sinks that had been absorbing it and starts to build up in the atmosphere. For the anaerobic microbes that had run the world, oxygen is a poison, and the Great Oxidation Event is probably the largest extinction in Earth’s history measured by the fraction of life affected.

It also breaks the climate. Oxygen destroys atmospheric methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, and the planet drops into the Huronian glaciation — a series of ice ages lasting on and off for 300 million years, quite possibly the first time ice reached the equator.

Out of that upheaval comes the eukaryotic cell. One cell takes up another — a bacterium that could use oxygen — and instead of digesting it, keeps it. That captive becomes the mitochondrion, and every plant, animal, fungus and seaweed since is descended from that merger. By the end of this era the first supercontinent we can map with confidence, Nuna, is assembled.
chapters.world: Cratons collide into Nuna (also called Columbia), the first reasonably well-established supercontinent, around 1.8 billion years ago.

events.title: The Great Oxidation Event
events.text: Free oxygen appears in the atmosphere for good. Banded iron formation peaks and then largely stops: the oceans have run out of dissolved iron to rust.

events.title: Huronian glaciation
events.text: With methane oxidised away, ice spreads possibly to the tropics — arguably the first Snowball Earth.

events.title: Eukaryotes
events.text: Cells with a nucleus and mitochondria. The Francevillian biota of Gabon, from about this age, may be the oldest large multicellular organisms, though the interpretation is debated.

events.title: Nuna assembles
events.text: A supercontinent forms; the Gunflint chert of Ontario preserves an exquisite microbial ecosystem from about this time.

featured.name: Grypania
featured.note: Coiled ribbons up to a few centimetres long — possibly the oldest large organism, and probably an alga.

featured.name: Gunflintia
featured.note: A filamentous microfossil from the 1.88-billion-year-old Gunflint chert, one of the first Precambrian fossils ever recognised.

featured.name: Francevillian biota
featured.note: Centimetre-scale disc and lobe shapes from Gabon, possibly colonial life 2.1 billion years ago.

chapters.name: Mesoproterozoic
chapters.lede: Six hundred million years of remarkably little change — and then sex, and the first thing that looks like a plant.
story: This stretch has a nickname among geologists: the Boring Billion. Carbon and oxygen isotopes stay flat, there are no global glaciations, sea level barely moves, and the supercontinent Nuna sits largely intact before reassembling as Rodinia. Oxygen appears to have stalled at a few percent of modern levels — enough for eukaryotes, not enough for animals.

Underneath the quiet, cells are getting more elaborate. Around 1.05 billion years ago, a red alga called *Bangiomorpha* is preserved in Arctic Canada in the act of doing something new: it has differentiated cell types, it is anchored to the seafloor, and it reproduces sexually. It is the oldest fossil that can be assigned to a living group with confidence, and the oldest good evidence for sex.

Meanwhile a second endosymbiosis has happened — a eukaryote swallows a cyanobacterium and keeps it as a chloroplast. Everything that photosynthesises in a nucleated cell, from kelp to oak trees, traces back to that event.
chapters.world: Nuna breaks up slowly and its pieces re-gather into Rodinia toward the end of the era, with the Grenville mountain belt marking the final collisions.

events.title: Oxygen stalls
events.text: Atmospheric oxygen holds at perhaps 1–4% of the modern level for hundreds of millions of years, apparently limited by nutrient supply and a sulphidic ocean.

events.title: Bangiomorpha
events.text: A red alga with specialised cells and sexual reproduction — the first fossil that can be placed in a modern group.

events.title: Rodinia assembles
events.text: The Grenville orogeny welds the continents together into a supercontinent that will sit astride the equator.

featured.name: Bangiomorpha
featured.note: A one-millimetre red alga from 1.05 billion years ago — the oldest fossil with differentiated cells and sex.

featured.name: Rafatazmia
featured.note: Filaments in 1.6-billion-year-old Indian phosphorite that may push crown-group red algae back further still.

featured.name: Acritarch
featured.note: A catch-all name for organic-walled microfossils — mostly the resting cysts of single-celled eukaryotes, and the workhorse of Precambrian biostratigraphy.

chapters.name: Tonian
chapters.lede: A supercontinent splits along its middle, flooding the world with new coastline — and the first animals appear, too small and soft to leave much behind.
story: Rodinia begins to rift apart around 825 million years ago. Rifting is a climate event as much as a tectonic one: fresh basalt weathers fast, drawing carbon dioxide out of the air, while new shallow seas bury organic carbon. Both push the planet toward the deep freeze that follows.

Molecular clocks — the rate at which genetic differences accumulate between living lineages — put the origin of animals somewhere in this period. The fossil record is thin, but there are biomarkers: 24-isopropylcholestane, a molecule made by demosponges, turns up in rocks of this age. The first animals were probably sponge-grade, millimetres across, and sitting on the seafloor.

Eukaryotes diversify visibly for the first time. Vase-shaped microfossils — the tests of amoebae — appear in the Grand Canyon and elsewhere, and give the first clear evidence of one eukaryote eating another.
chapters.world: Rodinia straddles the equator and starts to break apart, opening the first rift basins along what will become the margins of Laurentia.

events.title: Rodinia rifts
events.text: Large igneous provinces punch through the supercontinent and it begins to separate, opening new ocean basins.

events.title: Vase-shaped microfossils
events.text: Testate amoebae leave the first clear record of eukaryotes preying on eukaryotes.

events.title: Sponge biomarkers
events.text: Steroid molecules unique to demosponges appear in Omani rocks — chemical traces of the first animals.

featured.name: Melanocyrillium
featured.note: A vase-shaped microfossil — the shell of an amoeba, and evidence that eukaryotes were already eating each other.

featured.name: Demosponge
featured.note: The sponge lineage whose distinctive steroids appear in rocks of this age, before any sponge body fossil.

featured.name: Cladophora
featured.note: Green algae of this general kind were already photosynthesising in Tonian seas.

chapters.name: Cryogenian
chapters.lede: Twice, ice reaches the equator and stays for millions of years. Life survives, and comes out the other side about to become complicated.
story: The Sturtian glaciation begins around 717 million years ago and lasts, astonishingly, some 57 million years. Glacial deposits of this age are found on every continent, including at sea level in the tropics. The standard explanation is a runaway: ice reflects sunlight, cooling the planet, which grows more ice. Once the ice line reaches about 30° latitude the feedback runs away to the equator.

What ends it is volcanoes. With the water cycle shut down there is almost no weathering to remove carbon dioxide, so volcanic CO₂ builds up over millions of years until the greenhouse is strong enough to melt the ice — catastrophically fast, into a hothouse, leaving the strange "cap carbonates" that sit directly on glacial debris the world over.

It happens again: the Marinoan glaciation, ending about 635 million years ago. Life came through both, presumably in refuges — open water near volcanoes, meltwater ponds on the ice, the deep sea. And the oceans that followed were better oxygenated than any before them.
chapters.world: The rifted fragments of Rodinia sit mostly at low latitudes, which is part of why the runaway was possible: tropical continents weather fast and pull down CO₂.

events.title: Sturtian glaciation begins
events.text: Ice sheets reach sea level in the tropics and hold there for some 57 million years — the longest glaciation in Earth history.

events.title: The Sturtian ends
events.text: Volcanic CO₂ accumulates until the ice melts abruptly, leaving cap carbonates over glacial till.

events.title: Marinoan glaciation
events.text: A second snowball, shorter but just as extensive.

events.title: The last snowball melts
events.text: The Marinoan ends; ocean oxygen rises and the Ediacaran begins.

featured.name: Sponge
featured.note: Sponge-grade animals are the best candidates for what lived through the snowballs.

featured.name: Cyanobacteria
featured.note: Microbial mats persisted in refuges — meltwater ponds, volcanic vents, and cracks in the sea ice.

chapters.name: Ediacaran
chapters.lede: Soft, quilted, frond-like organisms up to a metre across cover the seafloor — the first big living things, and unlike anything alive now.
story: The Ediacaran biota appears about 575 million years ago in deep water off Newfoundland: fronds and spindles anchored to the mud, in water too dark for photosynthesis, apparently absorbing nutrients straight through their surfaces. They are built out of repeated quilted units on a fractal plan that no living group uses.

Later assemblages in the White Sea and Namibia include organisms that are easier to recognise. *Kimberella* looks like a mollusc and left scratch marks where it rasped a microbial mat. *Dickinsonia* left a series of resting traces as it moved and fed, and its fossils retain cholesterol — so it was an animal. Trace fossils show something burrowing.

At the very end, animals start to build hard parts. *Cloudina* and *Namacalathus* make small calcareous tubes and cups, and some *Cloudina* tubes have holes bored in them: the first predators, and the first arms race. Then the whole assemblage vanishes at the Cambrian boundary.
chapters.world: Rodinia’s fragments are drifting toward Gondwana; the Pan-African collisions are underway. Shallow seas are widespread and, for the first time, reliably oxygenated.

events.title: The ice ends
events.text: Cap carbonates blanket the world as the Marinoan glaciation collapses.

events.title: The Avalon assemblage
events.text: Fronds and spindles at Mistaken Point, Newfoundland — the oldest large complex organisms, preserved under volcanic ash.

events.title: The White Sea assemblage
events.text: Dickinsonia, Kimberella, Spriggina; movement, feeding traces, and the first grazing.

events.title: Skeletons and predators
events.text: Cloudina builds calcareous tubes — and something starts drilling holes in them.

events.title: The Ediacarans vanish
events.text: The assemblage disappears at the Cambrian boundary, whether by extinction, by being eaten, or by having its microbial-mat world churned up.

featured.name: Dickinsonia
featured.note: A flat, ribbed oval up to 1.4 m across that fed by resting on microbial mats. Its cholesterol proves it was an animal.

featured.name: Charnia
featured.note: A fern-like frond anchored in deep water, far below the reach of sunlight — the first complex fossil found in Precambrian rock.

featured.name: Kimberella
featured.note: A slug-like grazer that left paired scratch marks, and the best candidate for an early mollusc.

featured.name: Spriggina
featured.note: A segmented, head-bearing creature once read as an ancestral trilobite, now more cautiously left unplaced.

featured.name: Cloudina
featured.note: Stacked calcareous cones a few millimetres wide — among the first skeletons, and the first to be drilled by predators.

featured.name: Tribrachidium
featured.note: A disc with three raised arms in a spiral — a body plan with no three-fold living counterpart.

featured.name: Rangea
featured.note: The original "rangeomorph" frond, built from self-similar quilted branches repeated at four scales.

featured.name: Funisia
featured.note: Dense stands of tubes preserved in cohorts, suggesting sexual reproduction and larval settlement.

chapters.name: Cambrian
chapters.lede: In perhaps 20 million years almost every animal body plan still in use today appears in the fossil record, most of them already armoured, eyed, and hunting each other.
story: It starts with burrows. Through the earliest Cambrian, trace fossils get deeper, more varied and more three-dimensional as animals learn to dig. Then shells: tiny caps, tubes, spines and plates — the "small shelly fauna" — and then, around 521 million years ago, the trilobites, which will be the most conspicuous animals in the sea for the next 250 million years.

What makes the Cambrian legible is a handful of deposits that preserve soft tissue: Chengjiang in Yunnan, Sirius Passet in Greenland, and the Burgess Shale in British Columbia. In them the shelly fossils turn out to be a small minority. There are swimming predators a half-metre long with grasping appendages, five-eyed animals with a nozzle for a mouth, worms with spines and armour, and — small and easily missed — the first chordates.

The trigger is argued about endlessly: rising oxygen, the arrival of predation, the invention of eyes, the genetic toolkit reaching a threshold, or simply the fact that once anything is worth eating, everything else has to respond. Probably all of them, feeding back on each other. Ecology became an arms race and never stopped being one.
chapters.world: Gondwana is assembled in the south; Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia are separate, spread through the tropics. Sea level is high and warm shallow shelves are everywhere — which is where all of this happens.

events.title: The Cambrian begins
events.text: Defined by the first appearance of the complex burrow Treptichnus pedum — the boundary is drawn on a trace fossil, not a body.

events.title: Trilobites appear
events.text: Fully formed, with compound eyes, in several places at once.

events.title: Chengjiang
events.text: The Maotianshan Shales of Yunnan preserve a whole soft-bodied ecosystem, including the earliest fish-like chordates.

events.title: The Burgess Shale
events.text: A mudslide buries a reef-edge community in British Columbia and preserves it in extraordinary detail.

events.title: End-Cambrian extinctions
events.text: A series of pulses (the SPICE event and others) repeatedly cull trilobite faunas.

featured.name: Anomalocaris
featured.note: A metre-long swimming predator with grasping appendages and stalked eyes — the largest animal of its age.

featured.name: Opabinia
featured.note: Five eyes and a single flexible nozzle ending in a claw. When it was first described properly, the audience laughed.

featured.name: Hallucigenia
featured.note: A spined worm reconstructed upside down and back to front for decades before its head was identified.

featured.name: Wiwaxia
featured.note: An armoured slug-like animal covered in overlapping scales and long spines, related to molluscs or annelids.

featured.name: Marrella
featured.note: The most abundant Burgess Shale arthropod — small, delicate, and not a member of any surviving group.

featured.name: Pikaia
featured.note: A flattened, ribbon-like swimmer with a notochord: one of the first chordates, and so a distant relative of ours.

featured.name: Haikouichthys
featured.note: A 2.5-centimetre animal from Chengjiang with a skull, eyes and vertebral elements — arguably the first vertebrate.

featured.name: Olenellus
featured.note: A spiny trilobite of the early Cambrian, used to correlate rocks across Laurentia.

featured.name: Ottoia
featured.note: A priapulid worm that lived in a U-shaped burrow; gut contents show it ate hyoliths and, sometimes, other Ottoia.

featured.name: Aysheaia
featured.note: A soft, stubby-legged animal that probably grazed on sponges — close to the ancestry of velvet worms.

featured.name: Archaeocyatha
featured.note: Sponge-like animals that built the first true reefs, then went extinct before the Cambrian ended.

featured.name: Paradoxides
featured.note: A giant trilobite up to 40 cm long, characteristic of the Cambrian of Gondwana and Avalonia.

chapters.name: Ordovician
chapters.sub: Life fills the sea, then freezes
chapters.lede: Marine diversity triples, plants creep onto land, and then a glaciation kills roughly 85% of species.
story: The Cambrian invented the body plans; the Ordovician builds the ecosystems. In the Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event the number of marine families roughly triples. Reefs are taken over by corals and bryozoans, the seafloor fills with brachiopods and crinoid meadows, graptolites drift in the plankton, and enormous straight-shelled nautiloids — some over five metres — become the top predators.

On land, something quieter happens. Spores with the distinctive walls of land plants appear in Ordovician rocks: liverwort-grade plants, low and damp, without roots or vascular tissue. They begin, very slowly, to weather rock into soil, which draws down CO₂ — one candidate cause for what comes next.

At the end of the period Gondwana sits over the South Pole, ice sheets build, sea level falls by 100 metres or more, and the shallow shelves where nearly everything lived drain away. The Hirnantian extinction arrives in two pulses: cooling first, then the anoxic water that floods back as the ice melts. It is the second-worst extinction in Earth history.
chapters.world: Gondwana drifts over the South Pole. Laurentia sits on the equator under a warm shallow sea. The Iapetus Ocean between them begins to close.

events.title: The GOBE
events.text: Marine diversity climbs steeply for 25 million years, the largest sustained rise in the record.

events.title: Plants reach land
events.text: Cryptospores — the resistant spores of early land plants — appear worldwide.

events.title: The L-chondrite shower
events.text: An asteroid breakup in the main belt showers Earth with meteorites; fossil meteorites are common in Swedish limestone of this age.

events.title: Nautiloid giants
events.text: Cameroceras and Endoceras reach several metres — the largest animals yet to have lived.

events.title: Hirnantian glaciation and mass extinction
events.text: Ice on Gondwana, sea level crashes, and about 85% of species disappear in two pulses.

featured.name: Cameroceras
featured.note: A straight-shelled nautiloid, possibly six metres long, and the apex predator of Ordovician seas.

featured.name: Sacabambaspis
featured.note: An armoured jawless fish from Bolivia with a bony head shield and eyes set right at the front.

featured.name: Astraspis
featured.note: One of the first vertebrates with real bone, its head plated in star-patterned tubercles.

featured.name: Isotelus
featured.note: A trilobite that could exceed 70 cm — among the largest ever found.

featured.name: Didymograptus
featured.note: A tuning-fork graptolite; colonial hemichordates that drifted in the plankton and are superb for dating rocks.

featured.name: Orthoceras
featured.note: The archetypal straight cone shell, common enough that polished slabs of it are sold as ornaments.

featured.name: Promissum
featured.note: A conodont — an eel-like animal known mostly from its tooth apparatus, here preserved whole.

featured.name: Cystoidea
featured.note: Stalked, plated echinoderms that formed dense gardens on the Ordovician seafloor.

featured.name: Flexicalymene
featured.note: A trilobite that rolled into a ball when threatened; enrolled specimens are among the commonest Ordovician fossils.

featured.name: Rafinesquina
featured.note: A broad, thin brachiopod that lay concave-down on the seafloor in enormous numbers.

chapters.name: Silurian
chapters.sub: Life gets a backbone on land
chapters.lede: The ice melts, reefs rebuild, and the first plants with plumbing stand upright — with millipedes and scorpions right behind them.
story: Recovery is fast. Sea level rises again, and reefs — now built by tabulate and rugose corals and by stromatoporoid sponges — spread across the tropics. The Silurian is short, but it is when the sea gets crowded in a modern way: jawed fish appear and start to matter.

The decisive change is on land. *Cooksonia* is a few centimetres of forking green stem with a spore capsule on each tip and, critically, vascular tissue — cells stiffened with lignin that carry water upward. That is the invention that lets a plant stand up against gravity, and everything from ferns to redwoods follows from it.

Animals follow the plants. *Pneumodesmus newmani*, a millipede from Aberdeenshire, has spiracles — holes for breathing air — making it one of the oldest known air-breathing animals. In the water, eurypterids ("sea scorpions") become formidable: *Pterygotus* reached over 1.5 metres.
chapters.world: Laurentia and Baltica collide to form Laurussia, throwing up the Caledonian mountains; Gondwana remains in the south. Sea level is high again and the tropics are lined with reefs.

events.title: Recovery
events.text: Diversity rebuilds quickly after the Hirnantian, though with a changed cast.

events.title: Vascular plants
events.text: Cooksonia — forking stems with sporangia and lignified conducting tissue — establishes the vascular plant lineage.

events.title: Air breathers on land
events.text: Pneumodesmus, a millipede with spiracles, from Scotland.

events.title: Jawed fish diversify
events.text: Acanthodians and early bony fish spread; Guiyu oneiros from China is a complete early bony fish.

events.title: Sea scorpions peak
events.text: Eurypterids reach their greatest size and diversity.

featured.name: Cooksonia
featured.note: A few centimetres of forking stem tipped with spore capsules — the first vascular plant, and the ancestor of every tree.

featured.name: Pterygotus
featured.note: A eurypterid over 1.5 m long with paddle limbs and grasping claws — one of the largest arthropods that ever lived.

featured.name: Eurypterus
featured.note: The best-known sea scorpion, abundant in the lagoons of what is now New York State.

featured.name: Guiyu oneiros
featured.note: A complete early bony fish from China that mixes lobe-finned and ray-finned features.

featured.name: Birkenia
featured.note: A small jawless anaspid fish, streamlined and scaled, from Scottish rocks.

featured.name: Climatius
featured.note: A spiny "acanthodian" with up to six pairs of fin spines along its belly.

featured.name: Pneumodesmus
featured.note: A millipede with breathing holes — among the first animals known to have breathed air.

featured.name: Baragwanathia
featured.note: A clubmoss with real leaves and thick stems, surprisingly advanced for its age.

featured.name: Halysites
featured.note: The "chain coral", whose colonies form linked rings in Silurian reef limestone.

featured.name: Dalmanites
featured.note: A large-eyed trilobite with a long tail spine, common in Silurian shelf seas.

chapters.name: Devonian
chapters.sub: The age of fishes — and the first forests
chapters.lede: Armoured fish the size of cars patrol the seas, trees invent wood and roots, and something with fins and a neck crawls out of the water.
story: Fish take over. Placoderms — armoured, jawed, and often enormous — dominate, with *Dunkleosteus* reaching perhaps six metres and biting with shearing bony plates instead of teeth. Sharks appear in numbers, lobe-finned fish diversify, and the ray-finned fish that make up most of today’s species get started.

On land, plants solve the two remaining problems: roots and wood. *Archaeopteris* has a proper trunk with growth rings and a root system metres deep, and forms the first forests. Roots crack rock into soil, and the runoff of that new nutrient supply feeds algal blooms in the sea, stripping the water of oxygen — a plausible mechanism for the extinctions that punctuate the period.

And then the fin becomes a limb. *Eusthenopteron*, *Panderichthys*, *Tiktaalik*, *Acanthostega*, *Ichthyostega* — a sequence of fossils, mostly found since 1930, that shows the shoulder freeing itself from the skull, a neck appearing, and fins acquiring digits. The earliest tetrapods still had gills and probably still lived in water; the limbs came first, and the land came after.
chapters.world: Laurussia — the "Old Red Sandstone continent" — straddles the equator, its interior a vast arid floodplain. Gondwana is closing in from the south; the sea between them is warm and reef-rich.

events.title: The Rhynie chert
events.text: A hot spring in Scotland silicifies an entire early land ecosystem — plants, mites, springtails, and the oldest insect fragments.

events.title: The first forests
events.text: Archaeopteris grows real wood and deep roots; Gilboa in New York preserves stumps of the earliest trees.

events.title: Placoderms peak
events.text: Dunkleosteus and its relatives dominate marine food webs.

events.title: Kellwasser event
events.text: The Late Devonian extinction begins; reefs collapse and do not fully recover for over 100 million years.

events.title: Tetrapods
events.text: Acanthostega and Ichthyostega have limbs with digits — eight on each in Acanthostega’s case — but still breathe with gills.

events.title: Hangenberg event
events.text: A second crisis at the end of the period wipes out the placoderms entirely and resets vertebrate evolution.

featured.name: Dunkleosteus
featured.note: A placoderm up to six metres long, its head and thorax sheathed in bone, biting with self-sharpening plates.

featured.name: Tiktaalik
featured.note: A flat-headed fish with a neck, ribs and a wrist — the textbook intermediate between fish and tetrapod.

featured.name: Acanthostega
featured.note: An early tetrapod with eight digits per limb and internal gills: limbs evolved in the water, not on land.

featured.name: Ichthyostega
featured.note: A sturdier early tetrapod with a rib cage strong enough to support its body out of water.

featured.name: Eusthenopteron
featured.note: A lobe-finned fish whose fin bones line up with the humerus, radius and ulna of a limb.

featured.name: Archaeopteris
featured.note: The first modern-looking tree: a real trunk with growth rings, deep roots, and fern-like foliage.

featured.name: Bothriolepis
featured.note: A small armoured placoderm found on nearly every continent — one of the most abundant Devonian fossils.

featured.name: Cladoselache
featured.note: An early shark with a streamlined body and short jaws, preserved with its last meal intact.

featured.name: Rhyniognatha
featured.note: Jaw fragments from the Rhynie chert, argued to be the oldest known insect.

featured.name: Materpiscis
featured.note: A placoderm preserved with an embryo and umbilical cord — the oldest known live birth in a vertebrate.

featured.name: Titanichthys
featured.note: A placoderm as big as Dunkleosteus but toothless: a filter feeder.

featured.name: Elkinsia
featured.note: One of the earliest seed plants, freeing reproduction from standing water.

featured.name: Prototaxites
featured.note: A twenty-foot spire, probably a giant fungus, and the tallest organism on land for millions of years.

chapters.name: Carboniferous
chapters.lede: Swamp forests bury so much carbon that oxygen reaches 35% of the air — and dragonflies grow to the size of hawks.
story: Wet equatorial lowlands fill with forests of lycopsids — *Lepidodendron* and *Sigillaria*, 30 metres tall, with trunks armoured in diamond-patterned leaf scars — along with horsetails the size of trees and the first conifers on drier ground. When they fall into waterlogged swamp, they do not fully rot. Buried, compressed, and cooked, they become the coal that would later be dug up to run the Industrial Revolution.

Burying that much carbon without burning it pushes atmospheric oxygen to around 35%, the highest in Earth history, while CO₂ falls to near modern levels and the planet cools into the long Karoo ice age. High oxygen makes diffusion-limited breathing work at larger sizes, and arthropods take advantage: *Meganeura* had a 70-centimetre wingspan and *Arthropleura* was a two-and-a-half-metre millipede.

Vertebrates settle in. Amphibians of every shape fill the swamps, and somewhere in the middle of the period one lineage evolves the amniotic egg — a private pond with a shell — which finally severs reproduction from open water. *Hylonomus*, a lizard-shaped animal found inside fossil tree stumps in Nova Scotia, is among the first reptiles.
chapters.world: Gondwana and Laurussia converge and collide, raising the Appalachians, the Variscan belt and the Urals, and assembling Pangea. Ice covers much of the southern continent.

events.title: Romer’s gap
events.text: A thin stretch of tetrapod record after the Hangenberg extinction, now slowly being filled in.

events.title: Coal swamps
events.text: Vast wetland forests spread across the tropics; the Karoo glaciation grips the south.

events.title: The amniotic egg
events.text: Hylonomus and its relatives reproduce without water — the reptile line begins.

events.title: Oxygen peaks
events.text: Atmospheric O₂ reaches roughly 35%, and arthropods reach sizes never repeated.

events.title: Rainforest collapse
events.text: The coal forests fragment abruptly during an arid pulse, isolating populations and favouring reptiles over amphibians.

featured.name: Meganeura
featured.note: A griffinfly with a 70-centimetre wingspan, hunting other insects over the swamps.

featured.name: Arthropleura
featured.note: A millipede relative up to 2.5 metres long — the largest land invertebrate that has ever lived.

featured.name: Lepidodendron
featured.note: A 30-metre scale tree with a photosynthetic trunk that grew fast, reproduced once, and died.

featured.name: Sigillaria
featured.note: A lycopsid with a tall unbranched trunk and a crown of long grassy leaves.

featured.name: Calamites
featured.note: A horsetail the size of a tree, growing in dense stands along river channels.

featured.name: Hylonomus
featured.note: A 20-centimetre reptile found inside hollow lycopsid stumps — one of the earliest known amniotes.

featured.name: Pulmonoscorpius
featured.note: A scorpion 70 centimetres long from the Scottish Carboniferous.

featured.name: Crassigyrinus
featured.note: A long-bodied aquatic tetrapod with huge jaws and almost useless forelimbs.

featured.name: Eryops
featured.note: A metre-and-a-half amphibian built like a crocodile, hunting in and around water.

featured.name: Tullimonstrum
featured.note: The Tully Monster of Illinois — stalked eyes, a long proboscis with teeth, and still no agreed place on the tree of life.

featured.name: Helicoprion
featured.note: A shark relative whose lower jaw carried a spiral buzz-saw of teeth.

featured.name: Westlothiana
featured.note: A small, slender animal from Scotland close to the origin of the amniotes.

featured.name: Stethacanthus
featured.note: A shark with an anvil-shaped dorsal structure covered in tooth-like denticles.

chapters.name: Permian
chapters.lede: One supercontinent, one desert interior, a world of mammal ancestors — and then the worst extinction in the history of life.
story: Pangea is complete: a single landmass from pole to pole, with an interior so far from any ocean that it becomes one of the driest places the planet has ever had. The Karoo ice age fades and the world warms. Coal swamps give way to conifers, seed ferns and the *Glossopteris* flora that carpets Gondwana — the same fossil leaf found in India, Africa, Australia, South America and Antarctica, which is how Wegener knew the continents had moved.

The land belongs to synapsids — the lineage that leads to mammals. Early on they are sail-backed pelycosaurs like *Dimetrodon*; later come the therapsids, which stand with legs under the body, have differentiated teeth, and may well have been furry and warm-blooded. Alongside them are the armoured pareiasaurs and the first true reptile radiations.

Then, 252 million years ago, the Siberian Traps erupt through coal beds and evaporites, injecting carbon dioxide, methane and halogens into the atmosphere over perhaps a million years. Temperatures rise about 10°C, the oceans acidify, lose oxygen and fill with hydrogen sulphide. Something like 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates disappear. The trilobites end here. So do the eurypterids. It takes 10 million years for ecosystems to rebuild.
chapters.world: Pangea, surrounded by the single Panthalassic Ocean, with the Tethys Sea biting into its eastern side. The interior is desert; the coasts are seasonal and monsoonal.

events.title: Pangea complete
events.text: The last collisions weld the supercontinent together; the Karoo glaciation begins its long retreat.

events.title: Therapsids take over
events.text: Mammal-line synapsids with upright limbs and specialised teeth become the dominant land vertebrates.

events.title: Capitanian extinction
events.text: An earlier, smaller crisis, linked to the Emeishan Traps in China, removes many marine groups.

events.title: Siberian Traps
events.text: Millions of cubic kilometres of lava erupt through coal and salt deposits, releasing carbon and halogens.

events.title: The Great Dying
events.text: The end-Permian extinction: roughly 81% of marine species gone. Trilobites, eurypterids and blastoids end for good.

featured.name: Dimetrodon
featured.note: A sail-backed predator, and a synapsid — closer to us than to any dinosaur, despite being everyone’s idea of one.

featured.name: Inostrancevia
featured.note: A gorgonopsian with sabre-like canines, over three metres long, from the Russian Permian.

featured.name: Scutosaurus
featured.note: A heavily armoured, barrel-bodied pareiasaur that ate low-growing plants.

featured.name: Lystrosaurus
featured.note: A tusked, pig-sized dicynodont that survived the extinction and briefly made up most land vertebrates on Earth.

featured.name: Edaphosaurus
featured.note: A sail-backed herbivore with a broad body and crossbars on its sail spines.

featured.name: Diictodon
featured.note: A burrowing dicynodont known from thousands of specimens, sometimes found in pairs in spiral burrows.

featured.name: Estemmenosuchus
featured.note: A bulky herbivore with antler-like bony outgrowths on its skull.

featured.name: Gorgonops
featured.note: The archetypal sabre-toothed therapsid predator of the late Permian.

featured.name: Mesosaurus
featured.note: A small freshwater reptile found only in Brazil and southern Africa — early evidence that the two were once joined.

featured.name: Glossopteris
featured.note: The tongue-shaped leaf that carpeted Gondwana and helped prove continental drift.

featured.name: Coelurosauravus
featured.note: A reptile that glided on membranes stretched over rods grown from its skin, not from its ribs.

chapters.name: Triassic
chapters.lede: A hot, empty world refills — with dinosaurs, mammals, pterosaurs and the first reptiles to go back to the sea.
story: The early Triassic is a strange, impoverished place. Coal is absent from the record for millions of years — the "coal gap" — reefs are gone, and on land the dicynodont *Lystrosaurus* is so abundant it accounts for most vertebrate fossils found. Equatorial regions may have been too hot for large animals for stretches of time.

Recovery, when it comes, is inventive. Archosaurs split into two great branches: one leading to crocodiles, which for most of the Triassic are the more successful group, producing armoured herbivores and land predators; the other to pterosaurs and dinosaurs. The first dinosaurs, around 230 million years ago, are small, bipedal and unremarkable — a minor part of the fauna for 30 million years.

Two other things start here. Pterosaurs become the first vertebrates to fly under their own power. And small, shrew-like animals with a new jaw joint, a differentiated dentition and probably fur — the first mammals — appear near the end of the period, and spend the next 135 million years being small.
chapters.world: Pangea is still whole but starting to strain. The Tethys Ocean opens westward into the supercontinent; the interior stays arid and strongly monsoonal.

events.title: The empty world
events.text: Life after the Great Dying: low diversity, disaster taxa, no coal, no reefs.

events.title: Marine reptiles
events.text: Ichthyosaurs and sauropterygians return to the sea and diversify rapidly; Shonisaurus will reach 20 metres.

events.title: Modern corals
events.text: Scleractinian corals — the reef builders of today — appear and begin rebuilding reefs.

events.title: The first dinosaurs
events.text: Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus in Argentina: small, fast bipeds in a world still run by crocodile-line archosaurs.

events.title: The first mammals
events.text: Morganucodon and its relatives — small, nocturnal, insectivorous, with a new jaw joint and precise occlusion.

events.title: End-Triassic extinction
events.text: The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupts as Pangea starts to rift; about half of species disappear and the crocodile-line archosaurs are cut down, leaving the field to dinosaurs.

featured.name: Eoraptor
featured.note: A metre-long biped from Argentina, near the very base of the dinosaur family tree.

featured.name: Herrerasaurus
featured.note: An early predatory dinosaur with a sliding lower jaw joint for gripping prey.

featured.name: Coelophysis
featured.note: A slender, fast theropod known from a bone bed at Ghost Ranch containing hundreds of individuals.

featured.name: Plateosaurus
featured.note: A five-metre long-necked plant-eater, and one of the first really large dinosaurs.

featured.name: Morganucodon
featured.note: A shrew-sized animal with mammalian teeth and jaw joint — about as close to the first mammal as the record gets.

featured.name: Eudimorphodon
featured.note: An early pterosaur with a wingspan under a metre and multi-cusped teeth for catching fish.

featured.name: Shonisaurus
featured.note: An ichthyosaur up to 20 metres long, known from a Nevada site where dozens died together.

featured.name: Tanystropheus
featured.note: A marine reptile whose neck was longer than the rest of its body combined.

featured.name: Postosuchus
featured.note: A crocodile-line predator that walked on upright limbs and topped the food chain before dinosaurs did.

featured.name: Desmatosuchus
featured.note: An armoured aetosaur with huge shoulder spikes, built like a tank and eating plants.

featured.name: Placodus
featured.note: A marine reptile with protruding front teeth and flat crushing palate teeth for shellfish.

featured.name: Nothosaurus
featured.note: A long-bodied, seal-like fish hunter of the Tethys coasts.

featured.name: Lystrosaurus
featured.note: The survivor: for a while after the extinction, most land vertebrate fossils in the world belong to this one genus.

featured.name: Sharovipteryx
featured.note: A gliding reptile whose main membranes stretched between its hind legs.

chapters.name: Jurassic
chapters.lede: Pangea splits, the climate turns warm and wet, sauropods become the largest animals ever to walk, and a feathered dinosaur takes off.
story: Pangea comes apart. The Atlantic begins to open, Gondwana separates from Laurasia, and the flooded gaps between them become shallow seas full of ammonites, belemnites and marine reptiles. All that new coastline makes the world wetter, and the arid supercontinental interior gives way to forests of conifers, cycads, ginkgos and tree ferns.

With the crocodile-line archosaurs cut back by the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs expand into everything. Sauropods evolve into the largest land animals that have ever existed: a column-legged body plan with a long neck to reach food without moving, air-filled bones to keep the weight down, and a tiny head that never has to chew. *Brachiosaurus*, *Diplodocus* and *Apatosaurus* all come from the Morrison Formation of the American West.

And in a German lagoon, 150 million years ago, a small feathered dinosaur falls into the water and is buried in fine lime mud. *Archaeopteryx* has wings, flight feathers and a wishbone — and also teeth, claws on its hands, and a long bony tail. Found two years after *On the Origin of Species*, it remains the most famous transitional fossil ever collected.
chapters.world: The supercontinent divides. The Central Atlantic opens; the Tethys runs the width of the globe. High sea level floods Europe into an archipelago of islands and lagoons.

events.title: Dinosaurs inherit the land
events.text: With their rivals gone, dinosaur diversity and size climb steeply.

events.title: Toarcian ocean anoxia
events.text: A warming pulse strips oxygen from the oceans and lays down black shales across Europe.

events.title: The Atlantic opens
events.text: Seafloor spreading begins in earnest between the Americas and Africa.

events.title: The Morrison Formation
events.text: A seasonal floodplain in the American West preserves the classic sauropod-and-Allosaurus fauna.

events.title: Archaeopteryx
events.text: A feathered, winged dinosaur in the Solnhofen limestone — the link between dinosaurs and birds.

featured.name: Archaeopteryx
featured.note: Feathers, wings and a wishbone, plus teeth, clawed hands and a bony tail — the classic transitional fossil.

featured.name: Brachiosaurus
featured.note: A sauropod with front legs longer than its back legs, holding its head 12 metres up.

featured.name: Diplodocus
featured.note: Twenty-five metres of mostly neck and tail, weighing far less than its length suggests.

featured.name: Apatosaurus
featured.note: A heavily built sauropod whose tail may have been able to crack like a whip.

featured.name: Stegosaurus
featured.note: Two rows of plates along the back and four tail spikes — the plates probably for display and heat exchange.

featured.name: Allosaurus
featured.note: The dominant Morrison predator, nine metres long with blade-like teeth and ridges over its eyes.

featured.name: Compsognathus
featured.note: A chicken-sized theropod, once thought the smallest dinosaur, found with a lizard in its stomach.

featured.name: Ichthyosaurus
featured.note: A dolphin-shaped marine reptile with enormous eyes, giving birth to live young at sea.

featured.name: Plesiosaurus
featured.note: Four flippers and a long neck; the group that inadvertently gave the Loch Ness monster its shape.

featured.name: Liopleurodon
featured.note: A short-necked pliosaur with a skull well over a metre long, hunting other marine reptiles.

featured.name: Pterodactylus
featured.note: A small, long-jawed pterosaur, the first to be described and the source of the word "pterodactyl".

featured.name: Rhamphorhynchus
featured.note: A long-tailed pterosaur with a diamond-shaped vane on its tail tip.

featured.name: Anchiornis
featured.note: A four-winged feathered dinosaur whose fossilised melanosomes reveal a grey body, black wings and a red crest.

featured.name: Yi qi
featured.note: A pigeon-sized dinosaur that glided on bat-like membranes stretched from a long wrist bone.

featured.name: Castorocauda
featured.note: A swimming, beaver-tailed early mammal relative with preserved fur.

featured.name: Ammonite
featured.note: Coiled cephalopods so abundant and so fast-changing that they are used to date Jurassic rocks to within a few hundred thousand years.

chapters.name: Cretaceous
chapters.lede: The world turns green with flowers and loud with insects, dinosaurs reach their peak — and then, in an afternoon, it ends.
story: Flowering plants appear in the early Cretaceous and spread with remarkable speed, out-competing conifers and cycads across much of the world. They bring with them a co-evolutionary explosion: bees, butterflies, ants and the flowers that feed them diversify together, and the modern terrestrial ecosystem — flowers, pollinators, fruit, seed dispersers — takes shape.

It is a hothouse. There is no permanent polar ice; forests grow inside the Arctic Circle, and the mid-Cretaceous is one of the warmest intervals of the last 500 million years. Sea level is up to 250 metres higher than today, splitting North America down the middle with the Western Interior Seaway and drowning much of Europe.

Dinosaurs reach their greatest variety: tyrannosaurs, the horned and duck-billed herbivores, the enormous titanosaurs of the southern continents, and feathered dromaeosaurs. Birds and mammals are both diversifying quietly alongside them. Then a 10-kilometre asteroid strikes the Yucatán at about 20 km/s. The impact throws enough dust and sulphate into the stratosphere to shut down photosynthesis for months to years. Three-quarters of species die, including every dinosaur that was not a bird.
chapters.world: The Atlantic widens; India breaks free and races north; Africa and South America separate for good. Shallow seas cover a third of the continents.

events.title: Flowers
events.text: Angiosperms appear and begin their rapid spread; the Jehol biota of China preserves the earliest known flowering plants alongside feathered dinosaurs.

events.title: The Jehol biota
events.text: Volcanic ash in Liaoning preserves feathers, stomach contents and colour-bearing melanosomes in extraordinary detail.

events.title: Cenomanian–Turonian hothouse
events.text: Peak Cretaceous warmth and a global ocean anoxic event.

events.title: Tyrannosaurus
events.text: The last and largest tyrannosaur, in a North America split by an inland sea.

events.title: Deccan Traps
events.text: Enormous eruptions in India begin stressing the climate before the impact.

events.title: Chicxulub
events.text: A 10-kilometre asteroid hits the Yucatán. Wildfires, tsunamis, and years of darkness. 75% of species are gone.

featured.name: Tyrannosaurus
featured.note: Twelve metres, banana-sized teeth, and a bite that could crush bone — the most-studied dinosaur there is.

featured.name: Triceratops
featured.note: Three horns and a solid frill; one of the last dinosaurs to exist before the impact.

featured.name: Velociraptor
featured.note: Turkey-sized, feathered, with one sickle claw per foot — famously nothing like the films.

featured.name: Spinosaurus
featured.note: A fish-eating theropod longer than T. rex, with a huge sail and a paddle-like tail.

featured.name: Argentinosaurus
featured.note: A titanosaur estimated at 30-plus metres and 60-plus tonnes — among the largest land animals known.

featured.name: Ankylosaurus
featured.note: Armoured from snout to tail and swinging a bony club.

featured.name: Parasaurolophus
featured.note: A hadrosaur whose metre-long head crest was a resonating tube it could call through.

featured.name: Quetzalcoatlus
featured.note: A pterosaur the height of a giraffe with a ten-metre wingspan, likely stalking prey on foot.

featured.name: Mosasaurus
featured.note: A marine lizard up to 15 metres, with a second set of teeth on the palate.

featured.name: Pteranodon
featured.note: A crested, toothless pterosaur that soared over the Western Interior Seaway.

featured.name: Microraptor
featured.note: A four-winged dromaeosaur with iridescent black plumage that glided between trees.

featured.name: Confuciusornis
featured.note: An early bird with a true beak, known from thousands of specimens, many with long tail streamers.

featured.name: Repenomamus
featured.note: A badger-sized mammal found with a young dinosaur in its stomach — mammals were not only prey.

featured.name: Deinonychus
featured.note: The dinosaur whose 1969 description restarted the argument that dinosaurs were active and warm-blooded.

featured.name: Archaefructus
featured.note: One of the earliest known flowering plants, an aquatic herb from the Jehol lake beds.

featured.name: Sarcosuchus
featured.note: A twelve-metre crocodile relative with a bulbous snout tip, hunting in African rivers.

featured.name: Therizinosaurus
featured.note: A theropod with metre-long hand claws that it used on plants, not prey.

featured.name: Xiphactinus
featured.note: A five-metre bony fish, frequently found with an entire other fish inside it.

chapters.name: Paleocene
chapters.lede: Ferns, then forests. Mammals inherit an empty planet and, within ten million years, are producing animals the size of cows — and snakes that eat crocodiles.
story: The first thing that grows back is ferns. Sediments just above the impact layer are dominated by fern spores — the classic signature of a landscape stripped and recolonised. Within a few tens of thousands of years, forests return, and they return to a world with no large land animals in it at all.

Mammals had been around for 135 million years without exceeding badger size. Now, released from that ceiling, they radiate fast. Within four million years there are hoofed herbivores the size of cattle, and the first primate-like animals are in the trees. Birds also take their chance: flightless giants like *Gastornis* stand two metres tall.

It is hot, and getting hotter. At the very end of the epoch, roughly 56 million years ago, an enormous pulse of carbon enters the ocean-atmosphere system and global temperatures jump 5–8°C in a few thousand years. The Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum is the closest analogue the geological record offers to what humans are doing now — and even it released carbon roughly ten times more slowly.
chapters.world: The Atlantic keeps widening. North America and Europe are still connected across the north, which lets mammals move between them. India is closing on Asia. There is no polar ice.

events.title: The fern spike
events.text: Ferns dominate the recovering landscape immediately above the impact layer.

events.title: Mammals radiate
events.text: Placental mammal orders diversify rapidly into the vacated large-herbivore and predator niches.

events.title: Giant birds
events.text: Gastornis and its relatives stand two metres tall in the northern forests.

events.title: Titanoboa
events.text: A 13-metre snake in a Colombian rainforest so hot it implies year-round temperatures around 30–34°C.

events.title: The PETM
events.text: A carbon release warms the planet 5–8°C in a few thousand years, acidifies the ocean, and drives a deep-sea extinction.

featured.name: Titanoboa
featured.note: A 13-metre, one-tonne snake — the largest ever found — eating crocodile relatives in a Paleocene rainforest.

featured.name: Gastornis
featured.note: A two-metre flightless bird with an enormous beak, now thought to have been a plant-eater.

featured.name: Purgatorius
featured.note: A small, insect-and-fruit-eating animal near the base of the primate family tree.

featured.name: Plesiadapis
featured.note: A squirrel-like early primate relative with rodent-like front teeth.

featured.name: Coryphodon
featured.note: A hippo-shaped semi-aquatic herbivore, one of the first really large mammals.

featured.name: Carbonemys
featured.note: A freshwater turtle with a shell nearly two metres across, from the same deposits as Titanoboa.

featured.name: Barylambda
featured.note: A heavy, slow herbivore with a thick tail that may have propped it up to reach branches.

featured.name: Champsosaurus
featured.note: A gharial-shaped reptile that survived the extinction and kept fishing in northern rivers.

chapters.name: Eocene
chapters.lede: Palms grow in Alaska and crocodiles bask above the Arctic Circle. Then, over twenty million years, the planet cools into the ice ages we still live in.
story: The early Eocene is the warmest sustained climate of the last 65 million years. There is no ice at either pole. Rainforest reaches into Canada and Europe, Antarctica is forested, and the Arctic Ocean is a warm, brackish lake covered in freshwater fern. Modern mammal orders — bats, horses, whales, primates — all appear in this interval, most of them in the first few million years.

The best evidence is in two lake deposits. Messel Pit in Germany preserves mammals with fur, stomach contents and gut bacteria; Green River in Wyoming preserves fish, birds, insects and leaves in laminated shale. Between them they show a world of small horses no bigger than dogs, early bats already echolocating, and primates with grasping hands.

And whales go to sea. *Pakicetus* is a wolf-sized land animal with a whale’s inner ear; *Ambulocetus* swims like an otter; *Rodhocetus* has a tail fluke; and by the late Eocene *Basilosaurus* is an 18-metre fully aquatic predator with tiny, useless hind legs. Meanwhile the planet cools: India collides with Asia, the Himalayas rise, weathering pulls CO₂ down, and at 34 million years ago ice sheets appear on Antarctica for the first time in over 100 million years.
chapters.world: India slams into Asia and the Himalayas begin to rise. Australia and South America separate from Antarctica, opening the Southern Ocean and letting a current circle the pole.

events.title: Peak warmth
events.text: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum: no polar ice, forests at both poles.

events.title: The Azolla event
events.text: A freshwater fern blooms across a stagnant Arctic Ocean and, by sinking, may have drawn down enough CO₂ to help start the long cooling.

events.title: Messel and Green River
events.text: Two lake deposits preserve Eocene life in extraordinary completeness.

events.title: Whales go fully aquatic
events.text: Basilosaurus and Dorudon have flippers, flukes, and vestigial hind limbs.

events.title: Antarctic glaciation
events.text: The Eocene–Oligocene transition: ice sheets form on Antarctica and the Grande Coupure reshapes European faunas.

featured.name: Basilosaurus
featured.note: An 18-metre serpentine whale with hind legs the size of a human hand.

featured.name: Ambulocetus
featured.note: The "walking whale": an otter-like amphibious predator with a whale’s ear bones.

featured.name: Pakicetus
featured.note: A wolf-sized land animal whose skull already carries the hearing apparatus of a whale.

featured.name: Eohippus
featured.note: A dog-sized forest browser with four toes in front — the earliest horse.

featured.name: Uintatherium
featured.note: A rhino-sized herbivore with six blunt horns and sabre-like canines.

featured.name: Darwinius
featured.note: A superbly complete early primate from Messel, preserved down to its stomach contents.

featured.name: Icaronycteris
featured.note: An early bat with a claw on each finger, and an inner ear already built for echolocation.

featured.name: Andrewsarchus
featured.note: Known from a single metre-long skull; a huge hoofed carnivore related to whales and hippos.

featured.name: Arsinoitherium
featured.note: A rhino-like herbivore with two enormous hollow horns growing side by side.

featured.name: Moeritherium
featured.note: A tapir-shaped early relative of elephants, living in North African swamps.

featured.name: Palaeophis
featured.note: A giant sea snake found in Eocene marine rocks on several continents.

chapters.name: Oligocene
chapters.sub: Grass, and the biggest land mammal
chapters.lede: The world dries and opens out. Forests give way to grassland, and the largest land mammal that ever lived browses across central Asia.
story: With Antarctic ice established and CO₂ falling, the climate becomes cooler and much more seasonal. Closed forest breaks up into woodland and open country, and grasses — which had existed for tens of millions of years without dominating anything — begin to spread across continental interiors.

Grass is abrasive: it carries silica phytoliths that grind teeth down. Herbivores respond with taller crowns and more complex enamel, and legs built for running in the open rather than dodging between trees. Horses lose toes. The result is the beginning of the modern grazing fauna.

The extreme case is *Paraceratherium*, a hornless rhinoceros relative standing five metres at the shoulder and weighing perhaps 20 tonnes — the largest land mammal known. In the sea, whales split into the two groups alive today: the toothed whales, which by now echolocate, and the baleen whales, which begin filtering.
chapters.world: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current is fully established, thermally isolating Antarctica. The Alps and Himalayas continue to rise; the Tethys is reduced to the Mediterranean and its relics.

events.title: The Grande Coupure
events.text: Cooling and a land connection let Asian mammals replace much of the European fauna.

events.title: Grasslands spread
events.text: Open habitats expand; herbivore teeth get taller and legs get longer.

events.title: Paraceratherium
events.text: The largest land mammal known browses the woodlands of central Asia.

events.title: Baleen
events.text: Filter-feeding whales appear as cold, productive southern waters open up.

featured.name: Paraceratherium
featured.note: Five metres at the shoulder and perhaps 20 tonnes — the largest land mammal that has ever lived.

featured.name: Entelodon
featured.note: The "hell pig": a bison-sized omnivore with a bone-crushing bite and a face full of bony flanges.

featured.name: Mesohippus
featured.note: A three-toed horse the size of a large dog, with a longer face and better teeth than its ancestors.

featured.name: Aegyptopithecus
featured.note: An early ape-and-monkey ancestor from the Fayum of Egypt, with a small brain and large canines.

featured.name: Hyaenodon
featured.note: A widespread predator from an extinct order, with shearing teeth set further back in the jaw than a modern carnivore’s.

featured.name: Archaeotherium
featured.note: A long-legged entelodont with a huge head and a taste for carrion.

featured.name: Poebrotherium
featured.note: An early camel, gazelle-sized and built for open ground.

featured.name: Aetiocetus
featured.note: A whale with both teeth and the beginnings of baleen attachment.

chapters.name: Miocene
chapters.lede: Grasslands take over the continents, apes diversify across Africa and Eurasia, and the largest shark in history hunts whales.
story: The middle Miocene is a warm interval — the Miocene Climatic Optimum — followed by renewed cooling and drying. Grasslands expand enormously, and around 8 million years ago plants using the C4 photosynthetic pathway, better suited to low CO₂ and heat, spread across the tropics and remake the savanna.

This is the great age of apes. Dozens of genera range across Africa, Europe and Asia — *Proconsul*, *Ekembo*, *Dryopithecus*, *Sivapithecus*, and *Gigantopithecus*, which stood perhaps three metres tall. Somewhere in the late Miocene, in Africa, the lineage leading to chimpanzees and the lineage leading to us separate.

In the oceans, *Otodus megalodon* — up to 18 metres, with teeth the size of a hand — preys on whales. On land, elephant relatives with four tusks, clawed horse-relatives that walked on their knuckles, and the enormous flightless *Argentavis*, with a seven-metre wingspan, share a world already recognisably modern in its outlines.
chapters.world: Africa and India are locked onto Eurasia, the Tethys is destroyed, and the Alps, Himalayas and Andes are all rising. Around 6 million years ago the Mediterranean is cut off and very nearly dries out.

events.title: Apes radiate
events.text: Proconsul and its relatives spread through African forests.

events.title: The Miocene Climatic Optimum
events.text: A warm peak before the long slide into the ice ages.

events.title: Hominins and chimps split
events.text: Molecular and fossil evidence place the divergence somewhere between 9 and 6 million years ago.

events.title: The C4 revolution
events.text: Grasses using a low-CO₂ photosynthetic pathway spread worldwide, remaking tropical ecosystems.

events.title: The Messinian salinity crisis
events.text: The Mediterranean is cut off from the Atlantic and evaporates almost completely, leaving kilometres of salt.

featured.name: Otodus megalodon
featured.note: A shark up to 18 metres long, with teeth the size of a hand, that specialised in whales.

featured.name: Proconsul
featured.note: An early ape with no tail and a monkey-like body, from the forests of East Africa.

featured.name: Sivapithecus
featured.note: An Asian ape whose face is strikingly like an orangutan’s — and probably an orangutan ancestor.

featured.name: Gigantopithecus
featured.note: Known mostly from teeth and jaws; the largest ape that has ever existed.

featured.name: Deinotherium
featured.note: An elephant relative with tusks curving down and backward from its lower jaw.

featured.name: Gomphotherium
featured.note: A four-tusked elephant relative that spread across three continents.

featured.name: Argentavis
featured.note: A teratorn with a seven-metre wingspan, soaring over the Argentine pampas.

featured.name: Chalicotherium
featured.note: A horse relative with long clawed forelimbs that walked on its knuckles and pulled down branches.

featured.name: Thalassocnus
featured.note: A sloth that returned to the sea and grazed on seagrass along the Peruvian coast.

featured.name: Livyatan
featured.note: A sperm whale with functional teeth in both jaws, hunting other whales alongside megalodon.

featured.name: Synthetoceras
featured.note: A North American ruminant with a Y-shaped horn growing from its snout.

featured.name: Amphicyon
featured.note: The "bear-dog": a heavy predator combining features of both.

featured.name: Ekembo
featured.note: An early ape from Kenya, now separated from Proconsul, with a mix of monkey and ape traits.

chapters.name: Pliocene
chapters.lede: The Isthmus of Panama closes, two continents exchange their faunas, the northern ice sheets begin — and in East Africa something starts walking on two legs.
story: The Pliocene is close enough to today that the map looks familiar and cold enough that the ice ages are visibly coming. Early on it is still 2–3°C warmer than the pre-industrial world with CO₂ near 400 ppm — which is why it gets cited so often as an analogue for where we are heading — and sea level is perhaps 20 metres higher.

Panama rises from the sea, joining North and South America for the first time in tens of millions of years. The Great American Biotic Interchange follows: placentals move south in force, and South America’s endemic marsupial predators and strange native hoofed mammals mostly lose. Going the other way are armadillos, opossums, porcupines and giant ground sloths.

In East Africa, *Australopithecus* walks fully upright. The Laetoli footprints, 3.6 million years old, are three individuals crossing wet volcanic ash with a modern human stride — arches, no divergent big toe, heel first. The brain is still ape-sized. Bipedalism came first; the expensive brain came later.
chapters.world: Effectively the modern map, with one important difference: the Isthmus of Panama closes, cutting the Atlantic off from the Pacific and reorganising ocean circulation.

events.title: The Zanclean flood
events.text: The Atlantic breaks through Gibraltar and refills the Mediterranean, possibly within a couple of years.

events.title: Ardipithecus
events.text: A hominin with a grasping foot that still climbed but also walked upright.

events.title: The Laetoli footprints
events.text: Three hominins cross fresh volcanic ash in Tanzania and leave an unambiguous record of a modern walking gait.

events.title: Lucy
events.text: An Australopithecus afarensis skeleton from Hadar, 40% complete, that settled the argument about upright walking.

events.title: Northern ice sheets
events.text: Glaciation begins in the Northern Hemisphere; the first stone tools appear at about the same time.

featured.name: Australopithecus
featured.note: Ape-sized brain, human-like pelvis and feet — the genus that established upright walking.

featured.name: Ardipithecus
featured.note: An earlier hominin with a grasping big toe: at home both in the trees and on two legs.

featured.name: Megatherium
featured.note: A ground sloth the size of an elephant, able to rear up on its hind legs to feed.

featured.name: Glyptodon
featured.note: An armadillo relative as big as a small car, with a domed shell of fused bony plates.

featured.name: Smilodon
featured.note: The sabre-toothed cat: heavily built, ambush-hunting, with canines up to 28 centimetres.

featured.name: Titanis
featured.note: A "terror bird" that crossed into North America — two and a half metres tall with a hatchet-shaped beak.

featured.name: Macrauchenia
featured.note: A South American native ungulate with a trunk-like nose and no close living relatives.

featured.name: Toxodon
featured.note: A rhino-shaped South American herbivore that Darwin collected and could not place.

featured.name: Paranthropus
featured.note: A robust hominin with a bony crest anchoring huge chewing muscles, built for tough plant food.

chapters.name: Pleistocene
chapters.lede: Ice sheets advance and retreat fifty times, mammoths and giant sloths range across the continents, and one primate spreads to every one of them.
story: The Pleistocene is not one ice age but dozens, paced by slow wobbles in Earth’s orbit. Every hundred thousand years or so, ice sheets three kilometres thick spread over Canada and Scandinavia, sea level drops by 120 metres, Britain joins Europe, Siberia joins Alaska, and vast cold grassland — the mammoth steppe — stretches from Spain to the Yukon.

That steppe supports an extraordinary megafauna: woolly mammoths and woolly rhinos, cave lions and cave bears, giant deer with three-and-a-half-metre antlers, and in the Americas ground sloths, mastodons, sabre-toothed cats and *Arctodus*. Australia has marsupial lions, three-metre kangaroos, and *Diprotodon*, a wombat the size of a rhinoceros.

And there are several kinds of human. *Homo erectus* leaves Africa nearly two million years ago; Neanderthals occupy Europe and western Asia; Denisovans occupy the east; *Homo floresiensis* is a metre tall on an Indonesian island. *Homo sapiens* appears in Africa around 300,000 years ago and spreads worldwide after about 60,000. By the end of the epoch every other human lineage is gone, and so is most of the megafauna on every continent humans reached — with the timing of those extinctions tracking human arrival more closely than it tracks climate.
chapters.world: The modern map, repeatedly redrawn at the edges: with each glacial maximum, sea level falls 120 metres and land bridges open between Asia and America, Britain and Europe, and across Indonesia.

events.title: The ice ages begin
events.text: Northern ice sheets become a permanent feature and start their orbital rhythm.

events.title: Out of Africa, the first time
events.text: Homo erectus spreads into Eurasia, reaching Georgia, China and Java.

events.title: The mid-Pleistocene transition
events.text: Glacial cycles switch from 41,000 to 100,000 years and become much more severe.

events.title: Homo sapiens
events.text: The oldest fossils of our own species, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco.

events.title: The global expansion
events.text: Modern humans spread across Eurasia, reach Australia by 65,000 years ago and the Americas by at least 15,000.

events.title: The megafauna are gone
events.text: On every continent humans reached, most large mammals disappear within a few thousand years of arrival.

featured.name: Mammuthus
featured.note: The woolly mammoth: small ears, thick underwool, and a fat hump — a cold-adapted elephant that lasted on Wrangel Island until 4,000 years ago.

featured.name: Coelodonta
featured.note: The woolly rhinoceros, with a flattened front horn used to sweep snow off vegetation.

featured.name: Smilodon
featured.note: A sabre-toothed cat with forelimbs strong enough to pin prey while it delivered a precise throat bite.

featured.name: Megaloceros
featured.note: The "Irish elk": antlers up to 3.6 metres across, on a deer that ranged from Ireland to Siberia.

featured.name: Homo neanderthalensis
featured.note: Cold-adapted, big-brained, tool-making Europeans who buried their dead — and whose DNA is still in most of us.

featured.name: Homo erectus
featured.note: The first human to leave Africa, and the longest-lived human species so far.

featured.name: Ursus spelaeus
featured.note: The cave bear: a huge, largely vegetarian bear known from caves full of the bones of animals that died hibernating.

featured.name: Diprotodon
featured.note: The largest marsupial known, a three-tonne relative of wombats.

featured.name: Thylacoleo
featured.note: The marsupial lion, with bolt-cutter premolars and a thumb claw, and pound for pound the strongest bite of any mammal.

featured.name: Arctodus
featured.note: The short-faced bear, standing 3.5 metres upright, with long legs built for covering ground.

featured.name: Panthera leo
featured.note: Cave lions ranged from Spain to Alaska and appear in some of the oldest cave paintings.

featured.name: Doedicurus
featured.note: A glyptodont with a spiked, club-like tail it apparently used on rivals.

featured.name: Homo floresiensis
featured.note: A metre-tall human on Flores, making stone tools until about 50,000 years ago.

featured.name: Bison
featured.note: Steppe bison ranged across the mammoth steppe and are among the commonest animals in Ice Age cave art.

chapters.name: Holocene
chapters.lede: Eleven thousand years of unusually steady climate — long enough to invent farming, cities and writing, and to start changing the atmosphere ourselves.
story: The ice retreats and the climate settles into the most stable stretch in at least 100,000 years. Within two thousand years agriculture is invented independently in at least eleven places — wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent, rice and millet in China, maize and squash in Mesoamerica, potatoes in the Andes. Everything else follows from that: surplus, cities, writing, states.

The biological consequences are enormous. A handful of domesticated species expand to cover much of the planet’s land surface, and today the combined mass of livestock is far greater than that of all wild mammals. Species are moved between continents at a rate no land bridge ever matched, and extinction rates rise to somewhere between ten and a hundred times the long-term background.

And the carbon comes back. The coal buried in Carboniferous swamps, the oil from Cretaceous and Jurassic plankton, the gas from both, are being returned to the atmosphere in a couple of centuries. CO₂ is now above 420 ppm, higher than at any point in at least the last 3 million years, and rising about ten times faster than during the PETM — the fastest natural carbon release we can find in the record.
chapters.world: The map as we know it. Sea level rose about 120 metres as the ice melted, drowning the land bridges and creating the modern coastline roughly 7,000 years ago.

events.title: The Holocene begins
events.text: The Younger Dryas cold snap ends abruptly and the climate stabilises.

events.title: Agriculture
events.text: Wheat, barley, rice, maize and potatoes are domesticated independently around the world.

events.title: Writing
events.text: Cuneiform in Mesopotamia; the historical record begins.

events.title: Fossil carbon
events.text: Industrial coal burning starts returning Carboniferous carbon to the air.

events.title: The Great Acceleration
events.text: Population, energy use, and material flows all turn sharply upward after 1950.

events.title: Now
events.text: CO₂ above 420 ppm — the highest in at least 3 million years — and rising roughly ten times faster than during the PETM.

featured.name: Homo sapiens
featured.note: One species, every continent, and the first to alter the atmosphere deliberately enough to be visible in ice cores.

featured.name: Raphus cucullatus
featured.note: The dodo: a flightless pigeon on Mauritius, extinct within a century of humans arriving.

featured.name: Hydrodamalis gigas
featured.note: Steller’s sea cow, a nine-metre relative of the dugong, hunted out within 27 years of being described.

featured.name: Thylacinus cynocephalus
featured.note: The thylacine, the last of a marsupial predator lineage, shot out of Tasmania by 1936.

featured.name: Ectopistes migratorius
featured.note: The passenger pigeon went from billions of birds to none in about fifty years.

featured.name: Bos taurus
featured.note: Cattle: descended from the aurochs, and now with a combined mass many times that of all wild land mammals.

featured.name: Triticum
featured.note: Wheat: a grass whose domestication underwrites most of human civilisation.

featured.name: Canis lupus familiaris
featured.note: The dog, domesticated from wolves well before agriculture — the first species we changed.
